title: Capstone
tagline: Assemble everything you built into one shareable AI PM portfolio piece.
intro: Nothing new to learn this week — just assembly. You've built a scorecard, a prompt template, a guardrail file, a prototype brief, and a review rubric, all for the I-9 Completion Assistant. That's not a coincidence: it's meant to read as one coherent piece of AI PM work when you put it side by side.

scenario.context: This section pulls together what you built in Weeks 1 through 5, automatically, from what's saved in your browser.
scenario.brief: Five separate exercises don't obviously add up to anything. One document that walks a single feature — the I-9 Completion Assistant — from idea, through spec, through guardrails, through prototype, through review rubric, reads as exactly what an AI PM does day to day. Add a short closing reflection, then export the full portfolio piece as one Markdown file.

whatsNext.heading: What's next: the orchestrator model
whatsNext.thesis: The PM's job doesn't change — discover the right problem, define the right solution, get it built, get it adopted. What changes with AI is capacity. A PM who runs several scoped AI workstreams in parallel can sustain a depth of discovery, spec quality, and review rigor that used to take a team of analysts. The five skills you just practiced aren't isolated exercises — they're the building blocks of that model, applied one at a time. Once they're second nature, the same skills compose into running multiple scoped workstreams at once, with you as the orchestrator: scoping each one, reviewing its output, and deciding what becomes a commitment.

mapping.note: The value/viability/feasibility/usability judgment calls you made by hand are exactly what a scoring workstream needs a PM to define before it can run consistently across a large batch of ideas.
The structured prompt template you built is the seed of a scoped workstream that turns a validated idea into a build-ready spec.

Your guardrail file is a small version of the single source of truth — product definitions, constraints, past decisions — that every other workstream should draw from, so outputs don't drift from each other.
Going from spec to clickable outline without engineering is exactly the workstream that compresses 'is this the right direction' from weeks to hours.

mapping.week: Week 5 — Evaluating Output & the AI SDLC
mapping.note: Your rubric is the human-review checkpoint every workstream needs before its output becomes a commitment — 'agents draft, PMs decide' is the same rule you've been practicing all along.

whatsNext.note: A few workstreams in the fuller model — continuous competitive intelligence, syncing with a roadmap tool, synthesizing post-launch adoption data — need enterprise tool access and data pipelines beyond a personal Claude account and synthetic data, so they're not something to practice solo. Treat this page as a preview of where these five habits lead, not a new assignment — a fuller multi-workstream track is a natural next step once Weeks 1-5 feel automatic.

sections.heading: Closing reflection
sections.learning: The fastest way to make this stick is to run the same five steps on one real (non-sensitive, or fully within Gemini) feature idea in the next two weeks, before the habit fades — whether that's another I-9 & Onboarding feature, or a different Employer Services line like WOTC screening, offboarding, ACA reporting, unemployment cost management, or ID Watchdog.

example.text: Writing the guardrail file before handing anything to an agent is the habit I'm most likely to keep — I've been skipping straight from idea to ticket, and this gives engineering something concrete to build against. I want to try it next on our ACA reporting assistant, where a bad auto-filed form is a much bigger deal than a bad I-9 flag.
